verse.text: Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon, our beloved friend and coworker,
to Apphia our sister, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the assembly that meets in your house:
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution; here the group is small enough to meet in one household. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the reader sees one Greek word.

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
I always thank my God when I mention you in my prayers,
for I hear of your love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the holy ones.
verse.note: The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' is traditional, but now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Other translations use 'God's people' or 'his holy people'.

note.term: your love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the holy ones

verse.note: The translation keeps the Greek word order. Many interpreters read it as a crossed pattern: faith toward the Lord Jesus and love for all the holy ones, as in the parallel at Colossians 1:4. Others take both love and faith (in the sense of faithfulness) as directed to both the Lord and the holy ones.

verse.text: I pray that the partnership of your faith may become effective in the knowledge of every good thing that is in us for Christ.
verse.note: The Greek word means partnership or shared participation, and the phrase is among the most disputed in the letter. It may mean Philemon's participation in the faith alongside other believers, the generosity that flows from his faith, or the fellowship his faith creates; it probably does not mean telling others about one's faith, as 'sharing your faith' now suggests. 'Partnership' is chosen partly because Paul returns to the same word group in verse 17 ('partner'). Some manuscripts read 'in you' rather than 'in us' at the end of the verse.

verse.text: For I have had much joy and encouragement from your love, because the hearts of the holy ones have been refreshed through you, brother.
verse.note: The Greek word literally refers to the inner organs, which were thought of as the seat of the deepest feelings. It is not the usual word for 'heart' and is more visceral. Paul uses it three times in this short letter (verses 7, 12, 20), and the repetition is deliberate: Philemon, who has refreshed the hearts of others, is asked to refresh Paul's, and Onesimus is called Paul's very heart.

verse.text: Therefore, though I have great boldness in Christ to command you to do what is fitting,
yet because of love I appeal to you instead—being who I am, Paul, an old man and now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus.
verse.note: The word in the manuscripts means 'old man'. A closely similar word means 'ambassador', and the two spellings were sometimes interchanged in the period, so some scholars and a few translations read 'Paul, an ambassador and now also a prisoner'. Most translations keep 'old man', which suits an appeal that deliberately sets aside authority.

verse.text: I appeal to you for my child, whose father I became in my chains—Onesimus,
who was once useless to you but is now useful both to you and to me.

note.term: useless to you but is now useful

verse.note: The name Onesimus means 'useful' or 'beneficial' and was a common name for slaves. Paul plays on it with a pair of related Greek words, 'useless' and 'useful', which differ from the name itself but make the same point: the man has now become what his name says.

verse.text: I am sending him back to you—him who is my very heart.
I wanted to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he might serve me in my chains for the good news;
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, also used of imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' is the traditional rendering, but is now a religious term or a book title; many modern translations already alternate between the two.

verse.text: but I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that the good you do would not be forced but of your own free will.
For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while: so that you might have him back forever,
verse.note: This translation normally renders the word 'eternal', but here it is not attached to a noun: it describes how Philemon will have Onesimus back and is set against 'for a while' (literally 'for an hour'). English needs an adverb, and 'forever' is the traditional and natural one. The point is a relationship that, as between brothers in the Lord, outlasts this age, and not merely a slave returned for life.

verse.text: no longer as a slave but as more than a slave, a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

note.term: both in the flesh and in the Lord

verse.note: 'In the flesh' refers to ordinary human and social relationships, and 'in the Lord' to their shared belonging to Christ. Paul asks that Onesimus be treated as a brother in both spheres, not only in the assembly. Whether this amounts to a request to free him is disputed; Paul does not say so outright, though verse 21 hints that he expects more than he asks.

verse.text: So if you regard me as a partner, welcome him as you would me.
And if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account.
I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me your very self besides.
Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ.

note.term: let me have some benefit from you
note.traditional: let me have joy of thee; may I have this benefit from you

verse.note: The verb is the one from which the name Onesimus is formed, and it occurs only here in the New Testament. Most interpreters see a deliberate play on the name: Paul asks Philemon himself to be 'useful' to him.

verse.text: Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.
At the same time, prepare a guest room for me too, for I hope that through your prayers I will be granted to you.
Epaphras, my fellow captive in Christ Jesus, greets you,
verse.note: The word is different from the one Paul uses for himself as a 'prisoner' in verses 1 and 9. It properly means a fellow prisoner of war, in keeping with the military image of 'fellow soldier' in verse 2. Most translations render both words 'prisoner'; whether Epaphras was literally confined with Paul or the term is figurative is not certain.

verse.text: as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my coworkers.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
